title: CDC Declares Record Lettuce-Linked Parasite Outbreak Over After 12,883 Cases
excerpt: The multistate cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce is the largest on record; the FDA's contamination investigation continues.
body:
• The CDC declared the multistate cyclosporiasis outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce over on Friday, Sept. 11, after 12,883 confirmed cases across 21 states.
  • The outbreak is the largest on record in the U.S., causing at least 570 hospitalizations and two deaths, both reported in Michigan.
  • Traceback pointed to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico; the company recalled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico on July 18.
  • The FDA's investigation continues, with laboratory analysis of samples from Mexican growers pending and at least five other outbreak clusters still open.

Largest recorded outbreak ends after four months

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared an end Friday to the multistate outbreak of cyclosporiasis tied to iceberg lettuce, closing the book on the largest recorded surge of the parasitic illness in U.S. history. The outbreak sickened at least 12,883 people across 21 states since May 1, hospitalizing 570 and killing two, according to the CDC and FDA.

"The number of recent infections linked to the outbreak has significantly declined," the CDC said on its outbreak page. "The contaminated lettuce linked to this outbreak is no longer available in stores or restaurants." Federal officials say the best-by dates on all linked products have passed and there is no ongoing risk from that source.

Context & Background

Investigators first announced the multistate probe on July 16, after epidemiologic interviews pointed toward shredded iceberg lettuce served at some Taco Bell locations. A day later, traceback converged on a single supplier — Taylor Farms de Mexico — which initiated a voluntary recall on July 18 and pulled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market.

On August 20, the FDA began onsite inspections and sample collection at lettuce growers and a processing facility in Mexico, in coordination with Mexican officials. Michigan was hit hardest: about 1 in every 1,000 residents contracted cyclosporiasis, and both deaths were reported there. At the outbreak's peak, before the recall, more than 1,000 infections were occurring in a single day; by August, the average had fallen below two per day.

"FDA remains confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific Cyclospora outbreak is off the market. Although the outbreak is over, FDA's outbreak investigation remains ongoing."

— U.S. Food and Drug Administration, outbreak update

Impact & Analysis

The lettuce outbreak was only part of a grim summer for the parasite. In total, 19,595 cases of cyclosporiasis were reported across 49 states and Washington, D.C., as of early September, with 1,043 hospitalizations — and the CDC is still investigating several other case clusters whose sources have not been identified. At least five additional outbreaks remain under investigation on the FDA's foodborne illness page.

The true toll is almost certainly higher. Many people recover at home without testing, symptoms can take up to two weeks to appear after eating contaminated food, and confirmed cases carry a roughly six-week reporting lag — meaning states will keep adding cases to the CDC's count for weeks even with the outbreak declared over.

Cyclosporiasis is caused by the Cyclospora parasite and is known for causing watery, sometimes frequent diarrhea, along with loss of appetite, weight loss, stomach cramps, bloating, nausea, and fatigue. Symptoms can last from a few days to a month or longer without treatment, and can go away and return. Most people with healthy immune systems eventually recover without treatment, and the illness can be treated with antibiotics — but without treatment it can lead to dehydration and complications requiring hospital care.

Diaspora Angle

Fresh-produce outbreaks cut across every community, and South Asian households — where salads, chaats, and fresh garnishes are daily staples — are no exception. The practical takeaway is the oldest one in food safety: wash leafy greens thoroughly, even pre-washed bags, and when federal agencies name a recalled product, check the fridge rather than trusting memory. No recalled lettuce from this outbreak should remain on shelves, but the habit matters for the next one.

What's Next

The FDA will continue working with federal, state, and international partners to complete its investigation of how the lettuce became contaminated, with analysis of samples collected from Mexican growers still pending. The agency has also turned to post-outbreak prevention work aimed at stopping future Cyclospora surges as the historical season winds down. Meanwhile, the CDC's count of linked cases will keep ticking upward as delayed reports filter in — a statistical aftershock, not a new wave.
